props.title: Counter-Attack

sections.content: **Counter-Attack (1945)** (1945) stands as a tense World War II psychological thriller that broke new ground in depicting Soviet-American wartime alliance. Directed by Zoltan Korda, this claustrophobic drama stars Paul Muni and Marguerite Chapman trapped in a collapsed basement with German soldiers, creating a pressure-cooker scenario similar to the later **Lifeboat** (1944) by Hitchcock. The film's unique perspective showing Soviets as sympathetic protagonists marked a brief window of US-Soviet cooperation in Hollywood, alongside works like Mission to Moscow (1943) and **Song of Russia** (1944).

sections.content: The film's basement setting creates a microcosm of the larger war, with Paul Muni's Russian paratrooper character engaging in psychological warfare with his German captives. This confined space drama technique would influence later war films like **Stalag 17** (1953) and **The Young Lions** (1958), where limited locations amplify human conflict. Korda's direction emphasizes shadows and tight framing, borrowing from film noir techniques that were emerging in the mid-1940s. SUBHEAD: Wartime Politics in Hollywood

**Counter-Attack** (1945) represents a fascinating historical moment when Hollywood actively promoted Soviet alliance, before Cold War tensions emerged. This brief period produced several pro-Soviet films like **Days of Glory** (1944) starring Gregory Peck as a Russian guerrilla fighter. The shift in political climate would soon make such sympathetic Soviet portrayals impossible, leading to anti-communist films like **The Red Menace** (1949) and **I Was a Communist for the FBI** (1951).
